title: Is pork gelatin halal to eat?
headline: Fatwa bodies split on pork gelatin, with some banning it and others allowing it after full chemical transformation

summary.text: Most contemporary fatwa bodies in the Gulf and South Asia treat pork gelatin as haram, while several others, including Egypt's Dar al-Ifta and the Fiqh Council of North America, permit it when the transformation is complete. The split rests less on the Quran and Sunnah than on whether a forbidden substance can become lawful by chemical transformation and whether gelatin manufacture actually brings that about.

paragraphs.text: Four verses list the pig among forbidden foods: 2:173 and 16:115 forbid the flesh of swine, 5:3 forbids it again, and 6:145 adds that it is impure. Some scholars took the word rijs in 6:145 as a literal statement of physical impurity, so that every part of the pig shares the ruling, while others read it as a description of blame and vileness rather than ritual filth. The verses name flesh, not hide or bone, and the Permanent Committee answered this by noting that scholars agreed pig fat falls under the prohibition even though the verse says flesh.

The most directly relevant hadiths concern hides, tanning, and parts cut from an animal, because gelatin is extracted from hide and bone. The Prophet ﷺ said that any hide that has been tanned has become pure, a report graded sahih by Abu Ghuddah and al-Albani, and al-Tirmidhi adds that al-Shafi'i accepted the hadith but excluded the hides of the dog and the pig from it. He also said that whatever is cut from an animal while it is alive is dead flesh.

The Prophet ﷺ forbade the sale of pigs outright, and when asked about using the fat of dead animals for coating ships and treating hides, he refused. This is the hadith that anchors the position that the pig is impure in essence, since he refused even non-dietary uses of impure fat. The analogy for transformation comes from wine and vinegar: Anas reports that the Prophet ﷺ was asked about making vinegar from an alcoholic drink and said no.

Each school addresses whether an impure substance becomes pure when its essence changes, rather than gelatin by name. Ibn Abidin states that burning purifies by transformation, like wine turning to vinegar and like the pig that falls into a salt mine and becomes salt, yet the same school holds the pig impure in all its parts, and al-Marghinani's al-Hidaya excludes pig hide from the tanning hadith.

Al-Dasuqi reports that Sahnun and Ibn Abd al-Hakam held the hide of a dead animal, even a pig, becomes pure by tanning, and that Dardir rejected this. The school's broader principle, quoted from al-Qarafi, is that Allah restricted filth to certain objects on condition they carry certain impure properties, otherwise all objects are pure, and al-Hattab cites musk forming from congealed matter and blood turning into flesh as cases where transformation purifies.

Al-Nawawi states that an impure essence never becomes pure at all, except wine turning to vinegar and the hide of the dead animal by tanning, and al-Shirazi's Mughni al-Muhtaj treats purification by transformation as possible only in the case of the tanned hide. Ibn Qudama states the apparent view of the Hanbali madhhab that nothing impure becomes pure by transformation except wine turning to vinegar by itself, and he explicitly lists the pig that falls into a salt mine and becomes salt as remaining impure, though he notes a derived view that all impurities do become pure by transformation.

The apparent conflict is two stacked questions. The first is legal: whether istihalah is a general principle or a set of named exceptions. The Hanafi and Maliki reasoning, and the Hanbali takhrij, treat the impurity ruling as attached to a description that can cease, while the Shafi'i and relied-upon Hanbali reasoning treats the named cases as closed, so the pig-in-salt-mine example is decided against purification.

The second is factual, and most of the contemporary disagreement sits there. Those who forbid argue that what happens to collagen is hydrolysis and structural rearrangement, not transformation into a different substance, so the original protein identity remains. Those who permit rely on specialists who describe collagen and gelatin as entirely different in chemical structure, which is what istihalah means in fiqh, and both IslamQA and Dar al-Ifta Birmingham note that specialists themselves disagree on this point.

The Permanent Committee in Saudi Arabia held that gelatin prepared from something forbidden, such as the pig or its skin and bones, is forbidden, citing 5:3 and the consensus on pig fat. The Islamic Fiqh Council of the Muslim World League resolved that it is not permissible to use gelatin derived from pig sources in food, since alternatives exist, and IslamQA concluded it is not permissible to consume foods, drinks and medicines containing gelatin from pig skin or other impure substances.

Egypt's Dar al-Ifta ruled that foods containing pig derivatives are haram unless the nature of these substances has transformed into another form during industry or baking through chemical processing, in which case they become halal. The Fiqh Council of North America's position is that gelatin is permissible if it has undergone a chemical transformation that definitely changes its original features, which it identifies with istihalah.

The Assembly of Muslim Jurists of America noted that transformation is a strong opinion among many jurists, but that the pig is forbidden in its essence, and it leaned to the majority position that the pig's essence remains forbidden. Among Hanafi muftis, Darul Uloom Deoband and several online Dar al-Iftas hold that gelatin manufacture has not been shown to effect a real change of essence, so pork gelatin is to be avoided, while other Hanafi answers allow it if a complete transformation is established.
